title: Beast Games
synopsis: A thousand contestants. Millions in prize money. Cameras everywhere. You are contestant #482 and you have made it to the final ten. Don't look at the drones. Or do.

nodes.text: The arena is half-football-stadium, half-airport. Nine other contestants stand on circles taped to the ground. A producer in a polo shirt explains the next round with the calm of a man who has watched many people cry.

choices.text: Listen carefully — strategy starts at the rules
Scan the other nine

nodes.text: Each round eliminates two. The eliminated are paid a sum. The remaining split the bigger pot. The producers smile when they say 'except this round.'

choices.text: Ask what 'except this round' means
Don't react — pretend you expected it

nodes.text: You spot two reliable players — Marisol, who plans, and Devon, who reads people. You also spot one chaos agent named Brad who you suspect was cast for exactly this.

choices.text: Form a quiet pact with Marisol and Devon
Befriend Brad first; use his chaos
choices.consequence: Sometimes the wild card is your best play.

nodes.text: Stack soda crates higher than anyone. The producers have, you notice, given two contestants crates that wobble. Your stack is, mercifully, square.

choices.text: Win the round cleanly
Help Marisol's stack secretly while building yours

nodes.text: A producer, off-camera, leans in and offers you 'a small advantage' for a brief on-camera tantrum at Brad. You realize the show is, in part, a writers' room.

choices.text: Refuse the producer's offer
Take the advantage and overact mildly

nodes.text: A two-story plywood maze with cameras at every turn. The cameras click in a way that suggests they're tracking you in particular. Devon nudges you toward an unmarked door.

choices.text: Take the unmarked door
Take the marked path and stay legible

nodes.text: Round break. A sponsor wants you on Instagram doing a thirty-second clip with their energy drink. You realize your visibility has, accidentally, become an asset.

choices.text: Do the clip authentically
Politely decline; protect your image

nodes.text: Six players left. The producers have, terrifyingly, started using everyone's full name. The next round involves trust.

choices.text: Trust Marisol publicly
Trust nobody, smile at everyone

nodes.text: Brad pulls a stunt — slips a sleeping pill into someone's water bottle. He thinks it's funny. You realize the producers are not stopping him. They are recording his face.

choices.text: Pour the bottle out before someone drinks it
choices.consequence: Conscience is a budget you spend.

choices.text: Tell production and let them handle it
choices.consequence: Don't be the hero on camera.

nodes.text: Producers reveal a side quest: each remaining contestant nominates a charity, and a portion of their final winnings will go to it. Suddenly your strategy has a public face.

choices.text: Pick a charity you actually care about
Pick a charity that polls well

nodes.text: Brad, off-camera, breaks down and admits he's broke. The 'chaos' was him trying to be memorable for a sponsorship. He's, suddenly, a person.

choices.text: Help Brad through it
Be polite but stay focused
choices.consequence: Compassion has limits in a million-dollar game.

nodes.text: Marisol, you, Devon, and — Brad. The producers love it. The pot has, you realize, become genuinely life-changing.

choices.text: Honor the pact with Marisol and Devon
Break the pact at the right moment
choices.consequence: It is, after all, a game.

nodes.text: A reporter — between rounds — wants a comment about a video clip the show might 'leak.' You realize, again, the show is making its own news cycle.

choices.text: Give a careful, kind quote
Decline entirely

nodes.text: Stand on a beam. Hold a bag of sand. The first to drop loses. Devon's hands shake first. You can wait him out, or you can give him a graceful exit.

choices.text: Wait him out
Take the dive for him

nodes.text: If you split with Marisol you get less per person. If you break and win solo you get the most. If you break and lose you get the appearance fee. You have one more round to decide.

choices.text: Stick with the pact
Break and run for solo win

nodes.text: You and Marisol. The producers have built the moment perfectly. The lights, the music, the audience. She squeezes your hand. The host smiles.

choices.text: Propose splitting the pot live on air
Play the final game for the win

nodes.text: You go solo. Marisol is gracious on camera and, you realize, won't be next time. You win the final game. The check is enormous. The flight home is silent.

choices.text: Pay Marisol something off the books
Move on — it's a game

nodes.text: On air, you propose a split. The host hesitates. Marisol accepts. The audience goes wild. The producers — eventually — agree because the moment is gold.

choices.text: Use your platform after the show for the charity
Use your platform for your own next thing

nodes.text: You win. The check is six feet tall. There is confetti. Your knees, suddenly, are jelly. Marisol hugs you because she is, somehow, a better person than the game asked her to be.

choices.text: Share the win with the people who got you there
Take the win quietly and disappear for a year

nodes.text: The lawyers walk you through wiring instructions in a beige office. The cursor blinks. You decide, with a finger above the trackpad, what kind of person the money is going to make you.

choices.text: Cut checks to the people who got you here
Send one to your mother and disappear for a year

nodes.text: You spend the year touring with the charity. The money goes where you said it would. The follower count drops back down. You are, oddly, happier without the metrics. You write the producers a thank-you that is also goodbye.
You launch a small show of your own — kinder, weirder, less zero-sum. It does fine. It does, in time, very well. The Beast producers, surprisingly, recommend you to a network.

You write checks — to Marisol, to Devon, even to Brad. You pay your mother's house off. You set up a small fund for kids who applied to be on the show and didn't make it. It feels, you realize, like winning twice.

You disappear for a year. You hike, you sleep, you read books that are not self-help. When you come back you are a person who happened to win a thing once. You are, finally, not the contestant. You are you.
